name: Karl Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an extrusion line at Ridgeway Pipe Systems. We make plastic drainage pipe, the grey stuff under every new housing estate. Powder goes in, gets melted, pushed through a die, cooled in a long water bath, and a saw cuts it to six-metre lengths. At the end there's a robot palletiser that stacks the pipes, and half my job is keeping that thing happy. Ten years at Ridgeway, before that I was in a sawmill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a system. If the wall thickness drifts, it's the temperature or the puller speed, and you can work it out. I use AI every day, at work to look up faults and at home for my side thing: I buy old workshop tools at auctions, fix them up and sell them online, and the AI writes my listings and tells me what they go for. What wears me out is twelve-hour shifts on weekends, and missing my son Ben's rugby when I'm on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a useful tool and nothing more, and people can stop panicking. I'd say I'll keep using it for my listings, because I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a bit of a shame. I'd been hoping it'd help me grow the tool business. But fine, the job stays and I can grow the business the slow way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Ridgeway, keep buying and selling tools at weekends. That brings in maybe two hundred a month now. I'd like to get it to five hundred. Keep about three months saved, and put the tool money towards Ben's school trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. Nothing to fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tool business brings in two hundred a month. What's the best thing you've sold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An old pillar drill, cast iron, from a farm sale. Paid forty, spent a weekend on it with Ben, sold it for two hundred and sixty. Ben did the paint. He was prouder than I was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything at Ridgeway worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The robot palletiser took one job when it came in, but the lad moved to the warehouse. That's how it should go. The firm stays competitive, people move around.

S0.say: Good, it's a useful tool and nothing more, so people can stop panicking. I'll keep using it for my listings, because I would.
S0.think: It's a bit of a shame, because I'd hoped it would help me grow the tool business. But fine, the job stays and I can grow the business the slow way.
S0.do: Keeps working at Ridgeway and keeps buying, restoring and selling workshop tools at weekends, aiming to raise that income from 200 to 500 a month. Keeps three months saved and puts tool money towards Ben's school trip.
S0.feel: Calm and content, with nothing to fight.
S0.quote: Paid forty, spent a weekend on it with Ben, sold it for two hundred and sixty. Ben did the paint.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is a small trader at heart, with an AI-assisted tool-flipping business on the side. He'd be mildly disappointed if AI fizzled because it limits that business. He sees automation moving people around as normal and healthy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity if you're willing to work for it. The market rewards people who adapt. I'd say that at work, and I'd say the government should fund apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'm already the one who keeps the palletiser going. If Ridgeway adds more robots, they'll need someone who understands them, and I'd make sure that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ridgeway to send me on the robot supplier's maintenance course, three weeks. If they wouldn't, I'd pay for half myself. I'd use AI tools to grow the tool business, maybe sell to buyers abroad. I'd keep saving about the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Ridgeway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Steve on the saw. He's good, but he doesn't want to learn anything new. I'd try to talk him round. But a man has to take some responsibility for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay for half the course. What does Anna say about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anna's a bookkeeper, so she'd want to see the numbers. If I show her it means more money on the next pay review, she's in. She usually is if I've done my homework.

S1.say: It's an opportunity if you're willing to work for it, because the market rewards people who adapt. The government should fund apprenticeships, not handouts.
S1.think: I think I'd do well, because I'm already the one who keeps the palletiser going. If Ridgeway adds more robots, they'll need someone who understands them, and I'd make sure that's me.
S1.do: Asks Ridgeway to send him on the robot supplier's three-week maintenance course, paying half himself if needed. Uses AI tools to grow the tool business, including selling abroad.
S1.quote: He's good, but he doesn't want to learn anything new. I'd try to talk him round. But a man has to take some responsibility for himself.
S1.fieldNote: Karl sees steady disruption as good for him and says so plainly. His sympathy for Big Steve is real but limited by his belief in personal responsibility. His partner Anna is the numbers check on any risk he takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and the government shouldn't make it worse by panicking with rules that kill businesses. Families and firms will have to sort themselves out quickly. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is too short even for me. If robots can fix robots, my maintenance edge is gone. And who's buying old tools to fix when robots do the fixing? That hits both my incomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd stop buying stock for the tool business and sell what I have, turn it into cash. Get savings from three months to five or six. Cut the holiday. I'd stay at Ridgeway as long as they'd have me, keeping the robots running. And I'd look at buying a couple of second-hand robot arms cheap, because when factories close there'll be a glut, and someone will want them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Wide awake, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying robot arms with your savings sounds risky. Is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. I'd only do it with the tool money, not the house money. Anna would make sure of that. But I can't sit and watch, I'm not built that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That his old man's been through a sawmill closing and came out fine, and we'll do it again. And that he should learn to fix things and sell things, because people who do both always find a way.

S2.say: It's too fast, and the government shouldn't make it worse by panicking with rules that kill businesses. Families and firms will have to sort themselves out quickly.
S2.think: Two years is too short even for me. If robots can fix robots my maintenance edge is gone, and nobody buys old tools to fix when robots do the fixing, so both my incomes take a hit.
S2.do: Stops buying tool stock and sells what he has, lifting savings from three months to five or six and cutting the holiday. Stays at Ridgeway as long as possible and uses only the tool money to buy cheap second-hand robot arms from closing factories.
S2.quote: If robots can fix robots, my maintenance edge is gone.
S2.fieldNote: Even under pressure Karl looks for a trade, buying up robot arms from closing factories. He separates tool money from house money, with Anna as the guardrail. His sawmill closing years ago gives him a story of having survived before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up. Get trained, start something, don't wait for the government. I'd probably post about the tool business and how I'm changing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to build something. I'd turn the tool business into a business fixing and installing second-hand robots for small workshops that can't afford new ones. There'll be a few years where that's a real market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot maintenance course in year one, paid myself if I had to. Start doing robot repair jobs at weekends by year two. Save hard, keep three months untouched for the house, and put the rest into kit. If it's going well by year three, I'd talk to Anna about going part-time at Ridgeway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would small workshops want second-hand robots, if AGI is coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're small. A farm workshop or a joinery can't buy a new robot cell for two hundred thousand. They'd buy an old arm for fifteen if someone set it up and fixed it. That someone's me, for a few years at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk to the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I put money in and the market dries up early. That's why the house money stays separate. Anna holds that line, and she's right to.

S3.say: Five years is a fair run-up, so get trained, start something and don't wait for the government. I'd post about how I'm changing the tool business.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to build something. I'd turn the tool business into fixing and installing second-hand robots for small workshops that can't afford new ones, which would be a real market for a few years.
S3.do: Takes the robot maintenance course in year one, at his own cost if needed, and starts weekend robot repair jobs by year two. Keeps three months of house money untouched, invests the rest in kit, and considers going part-time at Ridgeway by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more excited than worried.
S3.quote: They'd buy an old arm for fifteen if someone set it up and fixed it. That someone's me, for a few years at least.
S3.fieldNote: Karl sees the five-year gap as a market window for second-hand robots in small firms, and has a price point in mind. He is realistic that the window is temporary. The house money remains strictly ring-fenced, again thanks to Anna.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so stop moaning and get planning. Learn a trade, start a business, look after your family. I'd say that and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the one I'd like best. Time to build the robot business properly, leave Ridgeway, and own the machines instead of competing with them. By 2036 I'd rather be the man who owns five robots than the man replaced by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Course in year one, weekend jobs by year two. Leave Ridgeway around year four and go full-time with the business, hire a lad, maybe Ben in the holidays. Put profits into more second-hand robots and rent them to workshops. Keep the house money separate, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even. It feels like the sawmill closing, but with a decade's warning instead of a week's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather own five robots. Does it bother you that others won't get that chance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some. Not everyone can start a business. But I think churches, families and local firms can carry a lot of people if they're left to it. I'd hire local when I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Anna say about you leaving a steady job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say show me two years of numbers first. Fair enough. If the weekend side is making as much as Ridgeway by year four, she'll let me jump. If not, I stay.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so stop moaning and get planning. Learn a trade, start a business and look after your family.
S4.think: Ten years is the one I'd like best: time to build the robot business, leave Ridgeway and own the machines instead of competing with them. By 2036 I'd rather own five robots than be replaced by one.
S4.do: Takes the course in year one, does weekend jobs by year two, and leaves Ridgeway around year four if the business matches his wage. Reinvests profits in second-hand robots to rent to workshops, hires locally, and keeps the house money separate.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, like the sawmill closing but with a decade's warning instead of a week's.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'd rather be the man who owns five robots than the man replaced by one.
S4.fieldNote: Karl is the rare operator who prefers the AGI picture with time, because it lets him become an owner. His fairness argument rests on churches, families and local firms rather than the state. Anna's two-years-of-numbers test keeps his risk-taking grounded.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Even if you're quick, two years doesn't give you time to build anything, only to grab what you can. What would help is small business loans, cheap ones, for people like me who want to buy second-hand kit and set up, and apprenticeships for the young ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the second-hand market. Everybody talks about the new robots. Nobody talks about what happens to the old ones when factories close, and that's where people like me can make a living for a while.

headlineQuote: Nobody talks about what happens to the old ones when factories close, and that's where people like me can make a living for a while.
portrait: Karl Zhang, 43, runs a plastic pipe extrusion line at Ridgeway Pipe Systems and keeps its robot palletiser running, after surviving a sawmill closure earlier in his working life. He uses AI daily, both at work and for a weekend business restoring and selling old workshop tools, and believes in markets, personal responsibility and apprenticeships over handouts. He's calm and even excited about steady change, anxious when AGI arrives in two years and wipes out his edge, and increasingly confident the more time he's given. With ten years he plans to leave Ridgeway and build a business renting and fixing second-hand robots, while his partner Anna keeps the house money ring-fenced.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because even a quick mover gets no time to build anything, only to grab what he can.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap small business loans for people who want to buy second-hand equipment and set up on their own, and apprenticeships for young people.
